Situation1: It seems your friend is confused about the meeting spot, and you need to send a message right now to confirm it.
Expectation2: Participate in civic life by staying informed, voting, and giving constructive feedback
Situation2: The city newsletter includes a short survey about bus routes open through next week.
Story: I glance at my phone, heart pounding a little. My friend, Jamie, just texted, “Wait, are we meeting at the café or the park?” I know how easily Jamie gets anxious when plans are unclear, and I promised myself I’d always be the friend who communicates openly, who helps clear up misunderstandings right away. I start typing a reply, but then my email pings—a reminder from the city about the bus route survey. I’ve been meaning to fill it out; I ride the bus every day, and I always tell myself I should participate more, give feedback, be a good citizen. The survey closes in an hour. I feel the pressure mounting—Jamie’s waiting, probably already worried, but the city needs input from people like me, too. My thumb hovers over the screen, torn between sending a quick message to Jamie or opening the survey link. I can’t do both at once, and I feel the weight of both expectations pressing in, demanding my attention right now.
